 Dengue deaths mount amid treatment delays
 Experts urge early diagnosis, timely referrals 
 Published : 20 October 2026
 • 
 Updated : 20 October 2026, 09:58
 • 
 DISEASE
 SHARE 
 Helemul Alam
 Helemul Alam 
 Four more people died of dengue yesterday, taking this year’s death toll to 352, as health experts warned that delayed hospitalisation, late diagnosis and inadequate treatment facilities were contributing to fatalities. 
 According to the Directorate General of Health Services, 1,14,251 dengue patients have been hospitalised nationwide this year.
 Tap here to add The Daily Star as a trusted source 
 Dhaka Medical College Hospital recorded the highest number of deaths at 99, followed by Khulna division with 65, Dhaka North City Corporation with 46, Chattogram division with 32, Mymensingh with 27, Barishal with 26, Rajshahi with 23, Rangpur with six and Sylhet with four.
 Health experts attributed the rising death toll to delayed hospitalisation and diagnosis, the absence of an effective three-tier dengue management system and increasing infections.
 A recent death review by the Institute of Epidemiology, Disease Control and Research (IEDCR), led by its Director Prof Quazi Ahmed Zaki, found that more than one-third of 119 patients reviewed died within a day of hospital admission.
 The review found that 62.5 percent died from dengue shock syndrome, 31.2 percent from expanded dengue syndrome, 16.1 percent from dengue with bleeding and 12.5 percent from other causes. Many patients also experienced diagnostic delays of at least three days.
 HM Nazmul Ahsan, associate professor at Shaheed Suhrawardy Medical College Hospital, said, “If 20 patients arrive, around 15 may be in shock. Approximately 90 percent of the patients we are receiving are critically ill.”
 He identified delayed referrals and long journeys from remote areas as major factors behind severe complications.
 Some patients travel five to six hours from district towns and other areas, reaching hospitals in shock or decompensated shock after their conditions deteriorate during the journey.
 Nazmul said patients should be stabilised before referral, including through intravenous access and appropriate fluid management. However, some facilities transferred patients without adequate initial treatment.
 Nazmul urged high-risk patients, including those with heart, lung, liver or kidney diseases, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease or obesity, as well as pregnant women, infants under one year and older adults, particularly those aged 60-65 and above, to seek hospital admission promptly after diagnosis.
 “Early hospitalisation is our main recommendation, particularly for high-risk patients. If we can reduce delays in seeking care and ensure appropriate treatment and stabilisation, we may be able to reduce the number of deaths and severe outcomes,” Nazmul said.
 Public health expert Mushtuq Hussain suggested piloting free dengue testing at existing primary-care facilities and referring vulnerable patients to hospitals when necessary.
 He said reducing deaths required community-level prevention, affordable early testing, timely referrals and proper hospital management rather than relying solely on tertiary hospitals.
